text: Privilege escalation sounds like a clever exploit, but on a real engagement it's almost always a misconfiguration review. Every category in this lesson is a known, documented class of configuration mistake that a hardening audit is specifically designed to catch — the same categories a vulnerability management program tracks and remediates on a schedule, whether or not anyone is actively testing them. Recognizing the category matters more than memorizing a specific command, because the category is what a defender actually fixes.

On Windows, four categories show up again and again. Weak service permissions, where a service running as LocalSystem has a writable binary path or registry key. Unquoted service paths, a path-parsing ambiguity that can run a file from an unintended, writable location. The AlwaysInstallElevated policy, which lets any local user install software with SYSTEM privileges. And stored or cached credentials sitting in scheduled tasks or unattended-install files — the same kind of secret-exposure problem course 10's DevSecOps content covers for source code repositories.

On Linux, the categories are just as well documented. SUID and SGID binaries that run with their owner's privileges rather than the caller's. Sudoers misconfigurations granting NOPASSWD on commands broad enough to read or write arbitrary files. World-writable cron jobs and scripts that run as root but can be edited by anyone. And kernel or capability misconfigurations — an outdated kernel with a known local privilege-escalation CVE, or a process granted more Linux capabilities than it actually needs.

Here's the connection that matters: every one of these categories is something course 8's Windows and Linux hardening content, and the CIS Benchmarks it covers, already tells a defender to check for — before anyone ever runs a test against them. A penetration test's privilege-escalation phase isn't discovering a brand-new risk category. It's proving that a specific, already-known risk category exists, unremediated, on a specific host right now, which is exactly the evidence a remediation team needs to actually prioritize the fix.

That reframes the whole phase. You're not hunting for clever new tricks — you're running the same checklist a good hardening audit runs, just with the motivation of proving real, unremediated risk on systems that are supposed to have already been reviewed. Next lesson moves from a single host's privileges to what that access can reach across the rest of the environment — the detection signatures a SOC watches for when that happens.
